v.why: Raising an already-large learning rate pushes Adam into divergence, causing large accuracy collapses (#9, #12, #18).
At tiny learning rates the network is undertrained after 243 epochs, so a step up gives clear gains (#1-4, #19).
Stepping down from a diverging learning rate recovers training and yields large improvements (#89-96).
Lowering an already-small learning rate further slows convergence and hurts accuracy, unlike the large gains seen at high rates.
Increasing an already-strong L2 penalty causes underfitting, with consistent drops (#73, #74, #83, #84).
At negligible alpha, a one-step increase barely changes the model, so the effect is near zero rather than negative (#69, #70, #82).
Deeper networks are less stable at high learning rates, so adding a layer there causes big drops (#57, #58, #63, #64).
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and stabilize training at high learning rates (#29, #30, #32).
Wider layers amplify the effective step size, so widening at high learning rates risks instability (#44).
At low, stable learning rates, extra depth adds capacity without instability and consistently helps (#53, #59, #60).

raw:
Ten hypotheses below, chosen from optimization knowledge and supported by the 100 single-seed experiments:

- **Learning rate is the main source of interaction.** Raising it helps when it starts low (#1–4, #19) and is catastrophic when it starts high (#9, #12, #18). Lowering it shows the mirror pattern (#89–96 versus #85–86).
- **Alpha penalizes more as it grows.** Raising alpha is roughly neutral at small values (#69, #70, #82) and strongly harmful at large ones (#73, #74, #83, #84).
- **Depth and width become risky at high learning rate.** Both edits fail badly there (#44, #57, #58, #63, #64) but help at low learning rate (#52, #53, #59, #60).
- **Larger batches calm high learning rates.** Raising batch size helps more when the learning rate is high (#29, #30), because it reduces gradient noise.
